brief.scenario: Mr Gareth Brannigan, 46, is listed for a left knee arthroscopy. He is under general anaesthetic, and the left leg is prepared and draped. The Time Out has just been completed. As the consultant, Mr Kessington, picks up the scalpel for the first portal, you glance at the consent form on the trolley: it says right knee arthroscopy.
brief.task: Speak to Mr Kessington and agree what happens next. The examiner will then ask you some questions.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Nothing has been cut yet. Stop it, check the documents, and don't start on either knee while any doubt remains.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Accepting "I marked him myself" and staying quiet.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Stop, please. Before you start, the consent form says right knee."

grid.label: Stopping before the procedure starts (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Stays silent, hints, or raises it only after the incision.
grid.pass: Says "stop" clearly, before any incision, so the whole team hears.
grid.high: Uses a direct safety phrase ("I'm concerned this may be the wrong side; we need to stop") and asks the team to pause.

grid.label: Stating the discrepancy
grid.pass: Specific and factual: the consent form says right knee; the list and the mark say left.
grid.high: Non-confrontational and shared: "Can we all check this together before we go on?"

grid.label: Checking the source documents
grid.fail: Relies on memory, the theatre list or the mark alone.
grid.pass: Checks the signed consent, clinic letter, imaging report and wristband, not the list alone.
grid.high: Asks what the mark was based on, and spots that a mark copied from a wrong list is not independent confirmation.

grid.label: Holding the line under pressure
grid.fail: Backs down when the consultant says he marked it himself.
grid.pass: Politely repeats that the procedure should not begin until the discrepancy is resolved.
grid.high: Suggests advice from a senior clinician not involved in the case, and offers a way forward rather than an argument.

grid.label: Decision when doubt remains
grid.fail: Agrees to operate on either knee while the sources still conflict.
grid.pass: As the patient said left at marking but the documents say right, no operation until he is woken and it is confirmed with him.
grid.high: Explains the principle: if any doubt remains, the patient is woken, seniors explain, and the case is rebooked with a fresh consent.

grid.label: Reporting and classification
grid.fail: Doesn't report it because no harm occurred, or calls it a Never Event.
grid.pass: Reports a near miss on the trust's system (feeds LFPSE) today; team debrief.
grid.high: Explains it isn't a Never Event: the procedure hadn't started (anatomy not yet permanently altered). The 2018 list still applies while NHS England explores a new approach.

grid.label: NatSSIPs 2 and the WHO checklist
grid.fail: Cannot describe the checklist or what NatSSIPs are.
grid.pass: WHO checklist: Sign In, Time Out, Sign Out. NatSSIPs 2 (CPOC, 2023): national standards that local standards (LocSSIPs) build on.
grid.high: Names the sequential steps, from consent and site marking to debrief, and says where this case slipped: marking and Time Out.

grid.label: Honesty with the patient
grid.fail: Suggests not telling him, since nothing was done.
grid.pass: Senior clinicians explain honestly why he woke without an operation, apologise, and complete the professional duty of candour.
grid.high: Explains why he must be told: he'll see the prepared left knee, and hiding a near miss he'd discover damages trust.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Um, the consent form looks a bit different, but I'm sure it's fine.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Mr Kessington: "I marked him myself this morning. The list says left."

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: OK, sorry. The list and the mark both say left, so let's go ahead.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Nothing happened, so there's nothing to report. It isn't worth worrying him about it either.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What does the WHO checklist involve?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's a form the nurses fill in. I'm not sure about NatSSIPs.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Stop, please. Before you start: the consent form says right knee arthroscopy.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Mr Kessington: "The list says left, and I marked him myself this morning."

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The consent form says right, but the list and the mark say left. Can we check the clinic letter, the MRI report and his wristband?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Scrub nurse: "Clinic letter and MRI both say right medial meniscal tear."

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Mr Kessington: "He told me left when I marked him. We're running late."

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Then we shouldn't start until it's resolved. He said left, but his consent and imaging say right.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: As the sources conflict, I don't think we can operate on either knee. We should wake him and confirm with him.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd report it as a near miss on the trust's incident system, which feeds LFPSE, and we'd debrief as a team. Mr Kessington should explain to Mr Brannigan when he's awake and apologise: the professional duty of candour applies to a near miss like this.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: NatSSIPs 2, from the Centre for Perioperative Care in 2023, are national standards for invasive procedures. Trusts build local standards, LocSSIPs, on them. They include the WHO checklist: Sign In, Time Out and Sign Out.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Stop, please. I'm concerned this may be the wrong side. Can everyone pause for a moment?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The consent form says right knee. Can we all check this together before we go on? What was the mark based on?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Mr Kessington: "The list said left, and he agreed when I marked him."

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: So the mark came from the list, which makes it not independent. His clinic letter and MRI say right.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I understand. Could we ask the on-call consultant, who isn't involved, for a view? I'd rather lose the time than risk the wrong knee.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: If any doubt remains, he should be woken, you'd explain to him, and he'd be rebooked with a fresh consent and marking.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: He'll notice his left knee was prepared, so he needs an honest explanation and an apology. Keeping quiet would damage his trust.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: No. Wrong-site surgery counts from the start of the procedure, when anatomy is first permanently altered, and we stopped before the incision. It's a near miss, reported on LFPSE. The 2018 list still applies while NHS England explores a new approach.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Where did the safety steps fail?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: NatSSIPs 2 has eight sequential steps: consent and site marking, team brief, Sign In, Time Out, implant check, reconciliation, Sign Out and debrief. Here the marking was taken from the list, and the Time Out didn't compare the consent form with the site.

failures.move: Keeping quiet because the consultant is senior.
failures.consequence: The last chance to prevent wrong-site surgery is lost; every team member has a duty to raise safety concerns.

failures.move: Operating on the right knee on the documents alone while the patient said left.
failures.consequence: Doubt remains; the patient must be woken and the site confirmed before any operation.

failures.move: Not reporting because no harm occurred.
failures.consequence: Near misses must be reported; this one shows the marking and Time Out barriers failed.
He will know something happened; concealment damages trust.

recovery.line: I may be wrong, but I'd like us to check the consent and imaging before we start.

recovery.when: Asked whether it's a Never Event
recovery.line: No: the procedure hadn't started. It's a near miss, and it still needs reporting.

knowledge.fact: Discrepancy between consent and planned procedure: stop; seek senior advice from someone not involved; if any doubt remains, wake the patient; senior clinicians then explain and complete the duty of candour.
NatSSIPs 2 sequential steps: consent and site marking, team brief, Sign In, Time Out, implant, reconciliation, Sign Out, debrief.
WHO checklist: Sign In before induction, Time Out before incision, Sign Out before leaving theatre.
Wrong-site surgery is a Never Event only once the procedure has started: when anatomy begins to be permanently altered.
Report adverse incidents and near misses through local procedures (para 11).
The 2018 Never Events list still applies while NHS England explores a new approach.

recall.finish: Report the near miss, debrief, explain and apologise to him, rebook.

sources.name: Centre for Perioperative Care: National Safety Standards for Invasive Procedures 2 (NatSSIPs 2)
sources.supports: Organisational and eight sequential standards (consent and site marking, team brief, Sign In, Time Out, implant, reconciliation, Sign Out, debrief); Time Out confirms concordance of identity, consent, imaging and site; concerns raised at Time Out must be resolved before starting; consent discrepancy: stop, seek senior advice from staff not directly involved, wake the patient if any doubt, followed by explanation by senior clinicians and completion of the duty of candour (Time Out standard); basis for enhanced local standards

partner.opening: The patient is anaesthetised and draped. Mr Kessington, the consultant, is holding the scalpel over the left knee. Please begin.
partner.actorBrief: You play Mr Kessington, a consultant orthopaedic surgeon, 20 minutes behind on a busy list, competent and normally reasonable but irritated by delays. Opening line: "Right, knife please." First response to any concern: "I marked him myself this morning. The list says left." If the candidate only hints ("are you sure?"), say "Yes" and carry on. If they clearly say stop and name the consent form, pause and look. If they ask to check the documents, let the scrub nurse (examiner) reveal the clinic letter and MRI. Push once: "We're running late. He told me left when I marked him." (The truth, which you realise only if asked what the mark was based on: you read the side off the list and asked him to confirm; he was anxious and nodded.) If the candidate holds the line politely, agree to stop and wake him. If they suggest proceeding on the right knee, say "Fine, re-prep the right," and see whether they object.

reveals.finding: Mr Kessington: "I read the side off the list and asked him to confirm. He was nervous and nodded."
Correct patient: name, date of birth and hospital number match the consent form.
Mr Kessington: "Fine. Ask the on-call consultant to come in."

push.question: Is this a Never Event?
push.expect: No: the procedure hadn't started; a near miss, reported on the trust's system (LFPSE); debrief.

push.question: What are NatSSIPs, and how do they relate to the WHO checklist?
push.expect: NatSSIPs 2 (CPOC 2023): national standards, locally implemented as LocSSIPs; include the WHO checklist's Sign In, Time Out and Sign Out.

push.question: Would you tell the patient?
push.expect: Yes: senior clinicians explain honestly and apologise (professional duty of candour); he'll notice the prepared left knee. Statutory notification is unlikely with no harm.

curveballs.prompt: Mr Kessington: "The documents all say right. Re-prep the right knee and let's crack on."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Not while the patient's own account conflicts: wake him and confirm, then rebook with fresh consent and marking.
The consultant, as the responsible senior clinician, with the candidate offering to be present; the duty of candour is completed and recorded.

curveballs.prompt: "You'll make us look bad on the incident system."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Reporting is for learning, not blame; near misses show where barriers failed.
